findings.title: Race condition: check-then-update allows over-redemption
findings.explanation: The plain SELECT takes no row lock, so under READ COMMITTED two concurrent requests can both see redemptions < max_redemptions and both run the unconditional UPDATE, pushing redemptions past max_redemptions. The original single UPDATE with the WHERE guard was atomic. Fix by using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the row, or (better) keep the guarded atomic UPDATE ... RETURNING and only run the diagnostic SELECT when rowCount === 0 to determine the reason for failure.

findings.title: UPDATE no longer guards the limit or expiry
findings.explanation: The UPDATE has no 'redemptions < max_redemptions' or expiry condition and its rowCount is not checked. Even with a lock, correctness depends entirely on the preceding application-side checks. Re-add the guard conditions to the UPDATE and verify rowCount so the DB enforces the invariant (also consider a CHECK constraint redemptions <= max_redemptions as a backstop).

findings.title: Expiry check uses app clock instead of DB clock
findings.explanation: The original used the database now(); the new code compares expires_at to the Node process's new Date(). Clock skew between app servers and the DB (or between instances) can make expiry decisions inconsistent with other parts of the system. Also, depending on the column type (timestamp without time zone) and pg type parsing, expires_at may be parsed in local time and shifted. Evaluate expiry in SQL (e.g. select expires_at <= now() AS expired) or ensure timestamptz is used.

findings.title: Same org can redeem repeatedly; no idempotency on retries
findings.explanation: Nothing prevents a client retry or double-click from consuming multiple redemptions for the same org, and a retry after a timeout will burn another use. If a coupon should be redeemable once per org, add a unique constraint on (code, org_id) and handle the conflict (return the existing result or a specific error such as coupon_already_redeemed). This is pre-existing but becomes more visible now that distinct errors are returned.

findings.title: API contract change breaks existing clients and exposes code enumeration
findings.explanation: The error body changes from 'coupon_unavailable' to three new codes. Existing clients that match on 'coupon_unavailable' will break; keep the old code for a deprecation period or document/communicate the change. Also, 'coupon_not_found' with 409 (rather than 404) is semantically off, and distinguishing unknown/expired/used-up codes makes coupon-code enumeration easier; ensure the endpoint is rate-limited. Consider whether revealing this to all callers is acceptable.

findings.title: Missing tests for the new branches and concurrency
findings.explanation: Add tests for each error path (not found, expired, used up, boundary where redemptions == max_redemptions - 1 and == max_redemptions, expires_at exactly now) and a concurrent-redemption test that proves the limit holds.

findings.title: Unused/loosely typed row data
findings.explanation: The row is untyped (any), so coupon.expires_at <= new Date() and the numeric comparisons are not type-checked; if max_redemptions or redemptions can come back as strings (bigint/numeric) the comparison would be wrong. Add a row type or do the comparison in SQL.

## Return specific errors when a coupon can't be redeemed

Support keeps asking why a coupon "didn't work". This splits the single UPDATE into a lookup plus explicit checks, so the API can say whether the code is unknown, expired, or used up. Still runs in one transaction.

 couponsRouter.post('/redeem', async (req, res) => {

-    if (updated.rowCount === 0) return null

+    if (coupon.expires_at && coupon.expires_at <= new Date()) return { error: 'coupon_expired' as const }
+    if (coupon.redemptions >= coupon.max_redemptions) return { error: 'coupon_used_up' as const }
